chapter: New York, Henderson and Charlie Johnson
title: Looking for gigs in New York and sitting in to build a name
summary: Gigs paid five or six dollars; he went round clubs leaving his name, sat in anywhere, and a player's reputation travelled faster than his name.

story.theme_name: Coming to New York: clubs, jams, and making it
story.community_name: Making it in New York: arrival, clubs and the scene

blocks.x: Well once you found a place to live, how did you make out finding a job?

Now, I think I can -- so I started looking around for, you know -- well at that time, gigs, you'd get a gig, five, six dollars a night. If you got into a ten dollar gig, man, you must have known Paul Whiteman! Or somebody, you know. Benny Goodman, or somebody, you know. Which did not happen. You didn't know those people. They didn't call anybody. So I started messing around, and the guy would call, and I'd introduce myself here and there, and back --
You'd go around to the clubs and just --
I'd go around to the clubs and say well,
my name is Herman Autrey, anything come, I'll call you. And --
Did you sit in when you went around?

I sat, sure, anywhere they wanted me to. And I could see anybody playing there I sat in and played. That was the thing then. If you played, that traveled faster than your name. Because -- they'd say there was a man here, oh, wow. There's a new guy in town, man.

Wow, the guy can blow. He did -- yes, what's his name? I don't know, but he saw -- you know (laughs.) Well where does he live? I'll get his phone number, and that got around, and that's what helped you. And then you would pass it around, and say well if anything happens, please call me, and that's the way you got known.
Did you know any people in New York at that time?

Well, different guys I'd met in different bands, yes. I did know, and it was celebrities. When I had met them in Philadelphia and other towns, yes, my name is Hemingwye (sic), you know, the English, the English. This is Joe, Little Joey. You know, you met -- well now keep going, Sonny, one day, and you never can tell, you know. You know, that whole thing. And so you keep moving.
That -- but the -- once in a while you meet a nice guy. He'd say okay, fellow, when you get to New York look me
up. I'll see what I can do for you. I'll try to help you. And he would. He'd mean -- he would mean it, you know. But usually he couldn't play either.

You know. So you had to keep pushing, pushing, pushing, pushing, just do the best you could do. So I said all right, thank you very much. And you keep plugging, keep plugging, but one day somebody will call you.
